title: Update on RISC-V Standards and Adoption at Hot Chips 2026
gist: SiFive's Hot Chips 2026 talk positions RISC-V, now 16 years old, as a maturing, profile-driven ISA uniquely suited to span host, device, and self-hosted roles in AI compute, with RVA23-compliant server silicon arriving in 2026 as the concrete proof point against lingering fragmentation, cost, and performance critiques.

insights.claim: RISC-V officially dates to May 18, 2010, giving it 16 years of history by Hot Chips 2026, with a timeline running from UC Berkeley origins through the RISC-V Foundation's founding to today's push into server processors with first RVA23 silicon.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: The maturation timeline (16 years, now reaching first server-class RVA23 silicon) is the benchmark for judging whether RISC-V server adoption is accelerating or still nascent relative to prior ISA cycles.
insights.quote: RISC-V marks its official birthday as May 18, 2010, giving the project 16 years of history by this Hot Chips.

insights.claim: SiFive frames RISC-V's core advantage as being a global, community-developed standard not tied to any single company's fortunes, which has produced a larger set of processor implementations than any prior ISA, from licensable IP cores down to open-source cores fitting in just 125 FPGA LUTs.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: An ISA not controlled by a single vendor lowers single-company/geopolitical dependency risk for chip designers, a factor investors should weigh when assessing RISC-V vs Arm/x86 supply-chain concentration risk.

insights.claim: RISC-V's specification is deliberately layered into base ISAs (fundamentals), extensions (bolt-on features), profiles (mandatory combinations per vertical), and platform standards (whole hardware subsystems beyond the ISA) to keep the many variants manageable.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: This layered structure is the mechanism RISC-V uses to balance flexibility with software portability; understanding it is a prerequisite for evaluating any RISC-V product's real compatibility claims.

insights.claim: Four base ISAs are ratified (RV32I, RV64I, RV32E, RV64E), differing by address width and register count, with further bases in development including a CHERI variant adding hardware capabilities and a future RV128 for 128-bit addressing.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: A future RV128 base signals RISC-V is architecting for addressing needs well beyond current 64-bit server/AI workloads, worth tracking as a long-horizon roadmap item.

insights.claim: RISC-V extension naming has evolved from early single-letter extensions (M for multiply/divide, V for vector, G as alias for common MAFD set) to a structured Z*-prefixed scheme where the letter after Z indicates the extension's category.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: The naming scheme shift reflects RISC-V's transition from an academic/simple project to an industrial-scale standard needing systematic namespace management as extension count grows.

insights.claim: RISC-V classifies its instruction encoding space into standard, reserved, custom, non-standard, and non-conforming categories, so vendor-specific features (e.g., the Xsfvqdotq extension) don't collide with future standard extensions.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: A governed custom-extension namespace lets silicon vendors differentiate with proprietary instructions while preserving a path back to standard compliance, reducing fragmentation risk from vendor lock-in extensions.

insights.claim: The RISC-V Vector (RVV) extension, ratified in 2021, adds 32 implementation-dependent vector registers and is vector-length agnostic, meaning a single compiled binary runs correctly across datapaths from 32-bit embedded parts up to 2048-bit AI accelerators without recompilation.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Vector-length agnosticism is a real software-portability advantage for AI/HPC workloads spanning embedded to accelerator-class silicon, potentially reducing the software fragmentation cost that has historically hurt niche ISAs.

insights.claim: RISC-V matrix support is being developed through complementary approaches grouped as AME, IME, and VME (differing in where matrix elements live and how they execute), plus a fast-track vector-based option, letting silicon vendors pick the implementation matching their datapath.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Multiple co-existing matrix-extension paths mean RISC-V AI accelerator vendors could diverge on matrix implementation choice, a fragmentation risk investors should watch as the matrix spec matures toward ratification.

themes.theme: RISC-V's role across the AI compute stack

insights.claim: SiFive positions AI compute organizations along a spectrum where a scalar/vector/matrix RISC-V core can sit in a CPU-style host, a device, or a fully self-hosted system, tracing this framing back to a 1968 paper on display processors.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: This host/device/self-hosted taxonomy is the lens SiFive wants adopted for evaluating where RISC-V cores fit in an AI system, useful for mapping which RISC-V vendors compete with CPU incumbents versus accelerator incumbents.

insights.claim: SiFive argues RISC-V is the only ISA that works well across every AI role simultaneously: as the host ISA (citing NVIDIA's CUDA stack port to RISC-V), as the device ISA inside many AI accelerators, and as a self-hosted ISA for edge AI and agentic CPUs.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: If NVIDIA's CUDA stack running on RISC-V as a host ISA gains traction, it validates RISC-V as viable inside NVIDIA's own AI compute ecosystem, a notable signal for RISC-V's credibility versus Arm/x86 hosts in AI servers.

insights.claim: RISC-V security starts at the ISA's lowest levels: physical memory protection (PMP) registers let machine mode control access from lower-privilege code, and RISC-V Worlds adds bus-level isolation by tagging transactions with a world ID for target-side permission checks.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Bus-level isolation via World IDs is a differentiated hardware security primitive that could matter for multi-tenant AI/cloud silicon designs evaluating RISC-V versus alternative ISAs for confidential compute.

insights.claim: Confidential compute is handled through supervisor domains, where a memory-resident page-based protection table lets machine mode isolate multiple supervisor or hypervisor stacks, and the IOMMU mirrors the same page-table format.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: IOMMU/CPU page-table format alignment simplifies building trusted-execution and confidential-VM stacks on RISC-V, relevant to cloud vendors evaluating RISC-V for confidential AI/cloud instances.

insights.claim: Beyond core mechanisms, RISC-V's security roadmap includes scalar and vector crypto, data-independent execution time, control-flow integrity, and pointer masking already defined, with CHERI, speculation barriers, memory tagging, and memory encryption contexts still in progress.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: A still-growing security feature backlog (CHERI, memory tagging, memory encryption) means RISC-V's security parity with mature server ISAs is not yet complete, a gap to track before treating it as enterprise/server-security-ready.

themes.theme: Software ecosystem profiles and server platform standardization

insights.claim: The RVA profile is RISC-V's answer to the tension between targeting a lowest-common-denominator baseline and adopting new features: it is a roadmap of mandatory ISA features hardware implementers commit to each generation so software can rely on them.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: RVA profiles are the mechanism that gives RISC-V software developers hardware guarantees comparable to what Arm/x86 baselines provide, directly enabling binary-distribution ecosystems like Android and Linux.

insights.claim: Ratified RVA generations for rich application-processor ecosystems (Android, Linux distros) run from RVA20 (capturing the earlier RV64GC baseline) through RVA22 to RVA23, ratified October 2024, which mandates vector extensions and a mandatory hypervisor.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: RVA23's mandatory vector and hypervisor support is the specific baseline that makes RISC-V server/cloud silicon viable in 2026; any RVA23-compliant chip is the concrete product signal to track for real adoption.

insights.claim: RVA releases split into major releases (RVA20, RVA23) that add substantial new mandatory functionality, and future minor releases that only add options, preserving forward compatibility so new standard software keeps running on hardware built to a previous major release.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: The major/minor release discipline is designed to prevent the fragmentation that has hurt other ISA ecosystems, a structural point relevant when assessing long-term software compatibility risk for RISC-V hardware investments.

insights.claim: RVB23, a separate ratified profile, targets application processors built with custom software via Yocto and OpenEmbedded rather than binary distributions, and future RVB profiles will evolve on their own independent cadence from RVA.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: A dedicated custom-build profile track (RVB) separate from the binary-distro track (RVA) shows RISC-V explicitly segmenting its standardization by deployment model, relevant for embedded/industrial versus consumer/server product planning.

insights.claim: New 'optimization guidance options' (Oilsm and Ovlt) let ISA strings describe performance expectations, not just features: Oilsm assumes misaligned loads/stores are handled efficiently, and Ovlt assumes microarchitectures optimize based on the dynamic vector-length register value rather than static loop shapes.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Adding performance-guidance metadata to ISA strings addresses a real software inefficiency (pessimistic coding around misaligned accesses), a small but concrete sign of RISC-V's spec process maturing toward production performance concerns.

insights.claim: A dedicated server platform spec requires RVA23-compliant processors plus standard RISC-V AIA interrupts, PCIe and IOMMU, UEFI and ACPI, TPM, and BMC management over MCTP, PLDM, Redfish, and IPMI, aligning RISC-V servers with established industry server standards.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Mandating industry-standard server firmware/management interfaces (UEFI, ACPI, Redfish, IPMI) means RISC-V servers are designed to slot into existing data-center management tooling rather than requiring bespoke stacks, lowering the operational adoption barrier for enterprises and hyperscalers.

insights.claim: The RVM profile extends the same profile logic down to microcontrollers, mandating extensions plus a subsystem with standard fast interrupts, nested sPMP protection, RISC-V Worlds security, and debug/trace support.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: Standardizing the microcontroller tier via RVM extends RISC-V's addressable market from servers down to embedded/IoT, broadening the total silicon volume opportunity beyond the AI/server headlines.

themes.theme: Fragmentation debate and competitive positioning versus Arm and x86

insights.claim: SiFive counters the common criticism that RISC-V is fragmented by comparing it to incumbents: x86 spans two vendors with different hypervisor and IOMMU specs, and Arm has shipped four distinct vector architectures, whereas RISC-V reuses a single vector extension across application cores, AI accelerators, and embedded parts.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: If accurate, this reframes the fragmentation narrative against RISC-V's favor relative to Arm's multiple vector ISAs, a talking point investors will hear repeated by RISC-V vendors to counter a key bear case.

insights.claim: SiFive/RISC-V International counters the 'too many extensions' complaint with counts: RISC-V has roughly 200 extensions versus about 400 for AArch64 and 800 for x86_64, arguing the extensions are managed to stay reusable.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: The raw extension-count comparison (200 vs 400 vs 800) is a specific, citable data point for rebutting the 'RISC-V is too complex' narrative in investor and technical due diligence conversations.

insights.claim: SiFive pushes back on the notion that RISC-V's appeal is purely lower cost, arguing that competitive pressure drives performance, power, and features too, and that RISC-V pairs freedom to innovate with a standard software stack that legacy ISAs cannot offer together.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: If RISC-V vendors can substantiate performance/power gains beyond cost, it strengthens the case for RISC-V displacing incumbents in performance-sensitive AI/server sockets rather than just low-cost embedded ones.

insights.claim: SiFive defends RISC-V's variable-length instruction encoding (often cited as a weakness) as a minor front-end consideration that improves code density, noting Arm and POWER have themselves moved toward prefix instructions as fixed-size encodings ran out of room.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: The claim that fixed-length incumbents (Arm, POWER) are drifting toward variable-length-like prefix schemes suggests convergence in ISA design, undercutting a long-standing anti-RISC-V performance critique.

insights.claim: SiFive rebuts the claim that RISC-V needs instruction fusion to be competitive by noting a single base RISC-V instruction already handles compare-and-branch (where x86 and Arm require fusion), and that optional fusion keeps simple instructions flexible without mandating complex macroinstructions.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: A design-level advantage (native compare-and-branch) rather than a fusion-dependent one, if true, is a technical differentiator relevant to evaluating RISC-V CPU microarchitecture claims versus x86/Arm cores.

insights.claim: The article's author is skeptical of SiFive's 'mythbusting' framing itself, arguing RISC-V is already used broadly in controllers and that what the ecosystem needs now is useful shipping products, not rhetorical defenses.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: An independent editorial pushback from the outlet itself signals that even RISC-V-friendly trade press wants to see execution (shipping RVA23 server products) over continued narrative-management from vendors.
insights.quote: I am not exactly a fan of the whole mythbusting thing. RISC-V is used for many controllers. We need useful products now.

insights.claim: The author's closing view is that RISC-V has moved from an academic project into a standardized, profiled ecosystem aimed squarely at servers and AI, with first RVA23 servers arriving in 2026 as the practical proof that the standards work is landing in real hardware.
insights.speaker: Vic A
insights.so_what: The arrival of first RVA23-compliant servers in 2026 is the concrete milestone investors should watch to judge whether RISC-V's standards progress is converting into real data-center deployments versus remaining a roadmap story.
insights.quote: First RVA23 servers arriving this year are the practical signal that the standards work documented in this talk is landing in real hardware.
